channel.title: Tangle - the good parts
channel.description: Tangle's daily edition cut down to Today's topic (the story, what the left and right are saying, and Isaac Saul's take) and Under the radar, plus Isaac's standalone essays. Sponsors, quick hits, extras, teasers, paywalled previews and the Sunday recap are left out.

item.title: The FlyDubai plane attack.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, do polls affect voters’ decisions?
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The FlyDubai attack. On Wednesday, the copilot of a FlyDubai commercial flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv allegedly attacked the plane’s captain and attempted to crash the aircraft in what Israeli officials have deemed an attempted terrorist attack. The captain, Smit Machchhar of India, was stabbed multiple times and seriously wounded but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing crew and passengers to detain the copilot. Two pilots on board as passengers then took control of the aircraft and landed it safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The attacker has been identified as an Omani national and is currently in custody in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

During the attack, the Boeing 737 MAX aircraft was subjected to extreme forces that exceeded its operational limits. The plane descended at a 39-degree angle (compared with a 3-degree angle in a standard descent), falling 17,400 feet in 92 seconds. When the other pilots on board managed to regain control, the aircraft lost part of its tail rudder, causing partial loss of control. The pilots kept the plane airborne for approximately one hour before landing at Tabuk Airport. 

A preliminary investigation has reportedly found that the copilot intended to take control of the aircraft and crash it into Israel’s Ben Gurion International Airport. Reuters also reported that the suspect operated a flight to Tel Aviv earlier this year with a similar goal of hijacking and crashing the aircraft but abandoned the plan for unknown reasons. Law enforcement officials said he had been suspended from flying by Oman Air in 2024 after he was found in possession of extremist materials. 

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said intelligence officials determined the copilot had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination,” but his precise motive is still unknown. Separately, United Arab Emirates Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi confirmed the hijacking was an attempted terrorist attack.

Today, we’ll share views from the right, left and Israeli writers, followed by Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right say the attempted attack underscores the broader state of play in the Middle East.
  • Others criticize the media’s coverage of the hijacking.

In The Free Press, Douglas Murray suggested “Israel is winning.”

“Most of all, the attack — and the successful averting of what could have been a mass-casualty terrorist event — is a reminder of something bigger: that Israel and the West remain at war with Islamic radicals, and that it is a war we are winning,” Murray wrote. “To some people, this reflection might seem counterintuitive. Each day’s news is filled with declarations of defeat. The online world is filled with shrill declarations that Israel has lost this war.

“With the hindsight of three years of war, we can now see more clearly how complete the devastation of Iran’s plans has been. Piece by piece, the government of Benjamin Netanyahu took apart the Iranian axis,” Murray said. “What happened in the skies above Saudi Arabia on Wednesday morning stands as a metaphor for three years of war. The Israelis saw an existential threat, took matters into their own hands, and decided their own course.”

In The Hill, Becket Adams argued that “caution is selective” among the news media.

“When it comes to crisis events, a cautious pose is always the smart play for a news organization. You never want to get ahead of the story — to prioritize being first ahead of being right,” Adams wrote. “But the care shown on this foiled hijacking story could not contrast more sharply with the Western press’s regular mishandling of allegations against Israel. The New York Times has, in particular, racked up a rather ignoble record in this area.

“The Times was among the first in October 2023 to misreport that Israel had bombed the Al-Ahli Arab Hospital, killing 500. Israel did no such thing. The rocket was misfired by the terrorist group Islamic Jihad, according to a U.S. assessment, and it did not even hit the hospital,” Adams said. “It is good, heartening even, that the Times handled last week’s foiled hijacking with care and caution… But where is this same seriousness when the allegations are directed at Israel?”

What the left is saying.
  • Some on the left suggest the incident threatens already tenuous Middle East relationships. 
  • Others praise the passengers for their quick action and resolve.

In The Atlantic, Graeme Wood said the incident has “huge implications.”

“Whether today’s near disaster was terrorism or merely attempted mass murder depends on the attacker’s motive. Either way, it is a public-relations catastrophe for Flydubai… Since the United Arab Emirates opened diplomatic relations with Israel in 2020, the airline has connected the two countries with few interruptions, even for acts of war and terror,” Wood wrote. “One possible political motive for the Flydubai incident would be to strain and punish the relationship between the two countries.”

“The next step will involve determining whether the pilot acted alone — not a good look for Flydubai, to have suicidal or terrorist pilots — or at someone’s behest. The latter possibility could, if confirmed, have serious implications, depending on who directed the attack,” Wood said. “Many have a motive: Sunni jihadists (al-Qaeda or the Islamic State), Hamas, and of course Iran and its proxies. This Mayday moment will have huge implications if any of these groups are involved.”

In The Forward, Dan Perry wrote “for a few terrifying minutes, Israelis were heroes again.”

“There is something refreshing about the simplicity of the story. The passengers were confronted with a danger that required immediate action, and some of them acted. Israelis watching the story unfold saw a familiar national trait emerge in circumstances where slogans had very little use,” Perry said. “For Israelis, that quality has long been part of the national mythology. The country was built around the idea that its people would have to improvise their way through circumstances that seemed to offer very little room for error.”

“Sadly, much of the world has encountered a very different Israeli stereotype in recent years. Israelis have increasingly become symbols in arguments about war, occupation, nationalism and international law,” Perry wrote. “Then came the FlyDubai flight… Israelis have been seen increasingly through the prism of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and sometimes through the actions of the government that happens to represent them. A plane full of passengers offers a different perspective.”

What Israeli writers are saying.
  • Some Israeli writers celebrate the collaboration between Israelis and Arabs on the flight. 
  • Others criticize the Israeli government for letting the Omani pilot pass through security measures.

In JNS, Fiamma Nirenstein said “heroic Israelis avert a new 9/11.”

“If there had not been ordinary Israelis on vacation aboard that plane, with their determined and well-organized will to survive, the world today might have been facing a new 9/11 in Tel Aviv,” Nirenstein wrote. “The alleged attacker was Omani. Oman has close relations with Iran, which maintains a strategic interest in the country because of its position overlooking the Strait of Hormuz and the entrance to the Persian Gulf. 

“The captain he allegedly attacked, by contrast, is a citizen of the United Arab Emirates — a friendly Arab country that signed the Abraham Accords with Israel,” Nirenstein said. “The contrast could hardly have been sharper: an alleged attacker apparently seeking destruction and an Emirati crew working alongside Israeli passengers to save lives. The passengers fought. The cabin crew helped them. Other pilots took control. Arabs and Israelis together prevented catastrophe.”

In The Jerusalem Post, Ben Caspit wrote “our security agencies… failed miserably.”

“A major failure occurred here — a massive one. A pilot — one whom Oman grounded for becoming radicalized and whom Morocco barred from flying due to his extremist Islamist views — found himself flying hundreds of Israelis to Israel,” Caspit wrote. “The Mossad has no way of knowing about every single jihadist who decides to kill Jews, provided that individual isn’t linked to an organized group or acting on orders from somewhere. If that is indeed the case, the Mossad bears less responsibility here.

“And yet, an Omani pilot – deemed ‘dangerous’ by the Omanis themselves – should not be flying to Israel without that information coming to the attention of Israeli authorities,” Caspit said. “Wherever Israeli flights take off from, there are always Israeli security personnel responsible for perimeter security… They operate alongside deep intelligence support, cooperation with local security forces, the vetting of anyone coming into contact with passenger security, and so on. They were there, and yet — it happened.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • It’s absurd that media outlets are being criticized for covering this story appropriately.
  • It’s also absurd to believe this attempted terrorist attack was a false flag.
  • Instead, this story is a reminder of the constant threats of violence Israelis live with.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

As news broke of the attempted terrorist attack on the FlyDubai plane, two other stories broke with it.

First was a controversy over how the story was reported. Prominent pundits, many on the right, criticized a New York Times tweet early on the morning of the attempted hijacking which read, “Breaking news: A plane flying from Dubai to Israel was diverted after an altercation between the pilot and co-pilot, Israeli officials said.” Other outlets had similarly ambiguous language. The BBC reported an “Israel-bound flight diverted after fight between pilots.” CTV News headlined its coverage, “Commercial flight from Dubai diverted, briefly raising hijacking concerns and prompting Israel to scramble warplanes.” Critics suggested this was an effort to obscure or downplay an attempt on Israeli lives — an obfuscation that might reinforce the dangers that Israelis face daily. 

The second controversy unfolded days later. Conspiracy theories exploded — predominantly on the left — suggesting the entire incident was a “false flag.” Perhaps the goal was to inspire national unity, or somehow make Netanyahu look good, or maybe use the event as an excuse for more national security. Ana Kasparian, who was a featured guest at last year’s “Tangle Live” event in Irvine, California, suggested that it was “weird” how “just yesterday Netanyahu was saying that the Iranians are going to carry out some sort of attack against Israel,” and “everyone was saying, ‘uh oh, here comes the false flag.’” She offered that she was “not suggesting” it was a false flag because she “doesn’t know yet,” but she thinks “it’s fishy.” Her co-host Cenk Uygur was less suggestive, using a segment to explain what “actually” happened with the FlyDubai plane, “how these things are done,” and “why might it be a false flag.” He went on to suggest that “they” might have found a mentally ill guy and allowed him to get on the plane with a knife. 

Both narratives bothered me for very different reasons. 

For starters, I don’t think there was anything wrong with the New York Times’ tweet. A lot of people don’t seem to understand how original reporting is done. When news breaks of a plane being diverted, and social media posts explode with claims of a struggle in the cockpit or a hijacking, an outlet like The New York Times is not going to report that without independent corroboration. Their job, as the paper of record, is to be careful — to be sure — not to amplify internet rumors. They’d never put something in print without at least getting some sources of their own.

Also, the Times’ reporting was not obscuring anything. As I documented on X, the offending social media post linked to a live page with updates. Before and after that tweet went out, The Times updated the story on that page, including comments from Israeli officials and the prime minister’s office discussing an attempted hijacking. It also made subsequent posts on X as it confirmed more details. Even under cynical reasoning, this particular criticism is nonsensical. If The Times could have been the first paper to report a hijacking of a plane full of Israelis to its audience — a story that would drive a boom in pageviews, subscribers, and citations — it would have.

The worst thing you can say about the paper and its journalists, which is a legitimate criticism, is that it has blasted out headlines (like the claim Israel killed 500 people bombing the al-Ahli Arab Hospital) based solely on Palestinian sources. I wrote an entire article criticizing the shoddy work of the hospital-attack story, and (predictably) The Times’ story completely fell apart. But the lesson from that incident isn’t to report faster or report more confidently based on potentially biased sources. The lesson is to be more careful to slow down and get it right. That’s what the Times did here, and nothing about its reporting was unethical or wrong. 

The other narrative, the one propagated by Kasparian and Uygur, was deeply disappointing. I like Ana, and I think she offers a lot of value as an independent political voice. But here, she offered an example of how deranged commentary about Israel has become. Kasparian and Uygur essentially speculated this attack was a false flag because it closely followed Netanyahu’s comments. Others are holding up even thinner evidence: Some X users claimed that the details of the story — from passengers getting into the cockpit to oxygen masks not deploying to the pictures of cups of water — indicate a conspiracy. These claims give off “jet fuel can’t melt steel beams so 9/11 was an inside job” vibes, and they are all easily debunkable. 

The story here is simple, even if it makes many people who distrust Israel very uncomfortable: There are people in the Middle East who want to kill Israelis and Jews. Examples of this kind of terrorism against Israelis and Jews are copious, and the FlyDubai example comes with copious videos, images, and firsthand accounts of bloodied pilots and passengers rushing the cockpit. All these details corroborate the story being reported not just in Israel or the United States but across the globe.

While information is still limited and in some cases vague, reporting about this copilot is pretty damning so far. He is an Omani national who was previously suspended from flying on Oman Air because he was deemed a security risk after being found in possession of extremist materials. His deleted social media posts pointed to “intense religious conservatism and misogyny,” ABC News reported. 

Also, he took an axe to his copilot and tried to down a plane with 174 passengers on board. 

An investigation will give us concrete details about what motivated the attack, but I don’t think we need to pretend the pieces are hard to put together. If anything doesn’t add up here, it’s how FlyDubai allowed this pilot in the cockpit at all. The UAE’s Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi — read: not an Israeli official — said on Saturday that it was an attempted act of terrorism. The attacker is an Omani national. Oman’s population is 95% Muslim. Israel is currently in live conflicts with several Muslim-majority nations throughout the region. The precise motivations will be fleshed out in an investigation, but I feel comfortable speculating that Islamic extremism, the conflicts in the Middle East, or some combination of the two will be involved. It is self-evident who the targets were.

In July, I wrote about how conspiracy theories are getting dumber. I’d argue both of these narratives add to the list of examples I shared in that piece. The New York Times is not avoiding front-page news it could break to the world because it’s scared to make Israel look like a victim. And Israel does not need to create false flag operations endangering its own citizens to create a mirage of danger — the danger is real, and Israelis live it every day. 

Take the survey: What’s your view on the incident? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The failed execution of Christa Pike.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: And the debate over capital punishment.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

Christa Pike and the death penalty. On Wednesday, Tennessee failed to execute Christa Pike after administering two doses of a lethal drug. Pike had been sentenced to death for her role in the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, and she is now hospitalized in critical condition. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) canceled the state’s final scheduled execution of 2026 and accepted the resignation of Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada. 

Back up: In 1995, Pike and her boyfriend lured Slemmer into the woods and attacked her, eventually bludgeoning her to death. The crime drew national attention due to the extent of Slemmer’s wounds and investigators’ suggestion that the killing was tied to the occult. Court documents said that Pike viewed Slemmer as a romantic rival; Pike confessed to the murder and was sentenced to death in 1996. 

Pike’s lawyers appealed the sentence, arguing that jurors may have decided differently had they been informed of physical and sexual abuse Pike suffered as a child. The attorneys also asked the Supreme Court to halt last week’s execution, saying it was likely to cause “severe mental suffering and superadded psychological terror under Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol.” The Court denied the appeal.

Tennessee’s death penalty protocol is to administer five grams of pentobarbital, a barbiturate that can depress breathing and circulatory function and lead to death. On Wednesday, according to witnesses, Pike complained of pain in her arm after prison officials administered an initial five-gram dose of pentobarbital. She was later given another dose and appeared to lose consciousness but continued breathing for another hour; eventually, witnesses were asked to leave the facility, and Pike was taken to the hospital. 

In a Saturday statement, Department of Correction Commissioner Strada maintained that the state followed all protocols in attempting to execute Pike but said he will step down “in the best interest” of the state. Separately, Gov. Lee ordered an independent investigation into the incident, which is Tennessee’s second failed execution this year. 

Pike’s attorneys criticized the state for its actions, saying it had been warned ahead of time that it was not prepared to carry out the execution. “The concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy,” they said.

Below are views from the left and right on the failed execution and the debate over the death penalty in the United States. Then, Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take. 

What the left is saying.
  • Many on the left say the failed execution highlights long-standing issues with the death penalty.
  • Some note Tennessee’s multiple failed executions this year.
  • Others argue the death penalty is immoral.

In Salon, Austin Sarat wrote “Christa Pike’s botched execution was not an isolated incident.”

“Such problems have occurred many other times, though generally they have not prevented executions from proceeding. The people tasked with the job of finding a usable vein and securing an IV are not phlebotomists with specialized training or nurses,” Sarat said. “In states like Tennessee, which does not carry out many lethal injection executions, members of the execution team do not have the chance to perfect their skill by using it a lot.”

“According to [American Medical Association] guidelines, doctors involved in lethal injections cannot choose injection sites, start IV lines to administer the lethal medicine or be involved in prescribing, preparing, administering, or supervising injection drugs or their doses or types,” Sarat wrote. “The result is that states have been forced to turn to unlicensed medical personnel. Hundreds of them have played a role in executions — but they have done so in the shadows. That is not good enough when someone’s life is being extinguished.”

In The Tennessean, Tacuma Roeback argued “Tennessee can’t get executions right.”

“Legal studies like this one have long called Tennessee’s capital punishment protocols into question, particularly when it comes to legal representation for defendants and the state’s administration of capital punishment,” Roeback said. “Before Pike, and before nine Tennessee lawmakers wrote Lee requesting a review of what went wrong in Carruthers’ execution, there were similar concerns about lethal injection protocols raised by another independent review four years ago. That review was supposed to fix things.”

“When the Tennessee Legislature resumes in January, it should push for a full, multi-year review of the TDOC and its death penalty protocol, including the method by which executions are administered,” Roeback wrote. “Given the demonstrated incompetence of how the death penalty is administered in this state, can we really trust that another review will result in substantive, corrective change?”

In USA Today, Rex Huppke called the failed execution “a moral stain on America.”

“Simply put, state and federal governments should not be in the business of killing people. Killing is messy, and things can go grotesquely wrong, as they did in Pike’s case,” Huppke said. “More important, though, killing is wrong. (I shouldn’t even have to type those words.) And the state deciding who among convicted criminals lives and who dies is morally obtuse.”

“There is no evidence the death penalty acts as a deterrent, yet there have already been 29 prisoners executed in the United States since January. We still haven’t reckoned with the fact that not wanting our government to kill criminals isn’t the same as wanting a murderer to live,” Huppke wrote. “The murderer is the one who did wrong, so what good comes from us doing wrong as well? I hope the horror of what happened to Pike at our hands shifts some thinking on the morality of the death penalty.”

What the right is saying.
  • Many on the right suggest the case shows the U.S. should return to previous methods of capital punishment.
  • Some argue that Pike’s history of abuse and mental health challenges should have ruled out a death sentence.
  • Others criticize legal hurdles that complicate and prolong executions.

In The Federalist, Hayden Daniel argued “Christa Pike shows it’s time to bring back firing squads.”

“In contrast to Lee’s limp-wristed act to deny justice even further by halting further executions, gubernatorial candidate and current Tennessee Sen. Marsha Blackburn said, ‘This situation is tragic. Christa Pike should have been executed long ago… The answer is simple: bring back the electric chair and deliver justice for these victims swiftly,’” Daniel said. “Blackburn is exactly right. People who commit especially heinous crimes should be dealt with via the death penalty and dealt with both efficiently and quickly.”

“The firing squad represents another execution method that we’ve nearly abandoned because of its supposed ‘barbarity,’ yet it stands as the very definition of swift and efficient… Death by firing squad comes in less than a minute, while death from lethal injection can take up to two hours, or not at all in Pike’s case,” Daniel wrote. “[Pike] shouldn’t have sat on death row for decades, and her botched execution undermines the pursuit of true justice — not only in her case but in all cases going forward.”

In National Review, Kathryn Jean Lopez wrote “the state as executioner is a moral failure — and turns out to be a practical one, too.”

“Pike was going to be the first woman executed in the state in over 200 years and the first person ‘in the modern era who was a teenager at the time of the offense,’ according to her clemency petition. This is barbaric,” Lopez said. “I don’t believe there is a circumstance in the United States in this day and age that warrants the death penalty. Like with just war, I think there could be a moral case and time. Not this time. Life in prison will do just fine.”

“Even if you do not agree with me: We should not be executing people with brain damage and with severe mental illness. Or who were severely abused as children,” Lopez wrote. “Child abuse happens when adults fail children. When they directly inflict pain on them, are indifferent to harm others are doing to them, or when they have not adequately protected them. Someone who was failed by the adults in her life from the beginning should not then be killed by the government.”

In the Washington Examiner, Zachary Faria described “how legislatures and the courts sabotage the death penalty.”

“State legislators and the courts have turned the death penalty into a grimly farcical process, feeding the cheapest arguments against it,” Faria said. “In March 1996, Pike was sentenced to death. Yet, Pike’s execution was not allowed to take place for another 30 years, thanks to the quagmire of appeals meant to bog down the process… The legal chicanery continued all the way to her execution date, when a federal appeals court momentarily halted the execution an hour before it was scheduled to take place.”

“This case will then be used to argue that the death penalty should be abolished. ‘It is more expensive than life imprisonment,’ you will hear, even though it is only more expensive because of the seemingly never-ending appeals that drag the process out for decades,” Faria wrote. “This legislative and judicial sabotage of the death penalty taints any debate about its merits, and it does so by denying justice to families like that of Slemmer.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • This case reinforces my opposition to the death penalty, which I view as both immoral and practically flawed.
  • We can abhor Pike’s botched execution and maintain sympathy for Slemmer’s family at the same time.
  • The simplest way to avoid more situations like this is to end capital punishment.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

A hospital is trying to keep a woman alive so the Tennessee government can try to kill her again.

That’s the dark, absurd situation created by the widespread acceptance of a system that allows the government to take the lives of its own citizens.

Longtime readers of Tangle will know that my most extreme political position is that I am anti-prison. I don’t believe we should release all the criminals into the streets — in fact, I don’t know of a better alternative for how to handle people who have proven themselves unfit for society. So, for now, I accept that prisons are necessary. But I do know that locking a human being in an 8x8 foot cage as a form of “justice” feels incredibly bleak, counterproductive, and inhumane. It’s a system that values punishment over civil liberties in the name of public safety, and the blackest parts of the soul push to hand out that sort of punishment.

So, unsurprisingly, I also oppose the death penalty. 

Here, my argument is much more straightforward and defensible, because there is an alternative: Don’t allow our government to kill prisoners. Rather than debating the merits of executing someone like Christa Pike, or having arguments about whether someone who slit another person’s throat is worthy of sympathy, I choose to draw a simple line in the sand: Killing is immoral. There are reasons to cross that line in the sand — a police officer killing someone in the midst of a mass shooting, or someone defending themselves or others from legitimate lethal threats. But we have laws and systems to navigate those exceptions.

That’s the principled argument against the death penalty. Citizens don’t get to kill other people, so the justice system shouldn’t get to kill citizens. The practical argument, as I’ve laid out before, is that the government has almost certainly executed innocent people, and it has come terrifyingly close to executing innocents hundreds of times before. It’s so common that trying to free people wrongfully put on death row has become a cottage industry — and those appeals often succeed. How many government killings of innocent citizens are we willing to accept? The answer should be zero. But the only way to guarantee that is to end the practice. 

But if none of that resonates, I have other practical arguments. The government is (evidently) bad at killing people, the legal process costs us more money than keeping inmates alive, and the death penalty itself isn’t actually a deterrent to heinous crime. So on top of the moral issue, it’s also carried out against the wrong people, in the wrong way, and to no practical end.

It really doesn’t matter if you want to mete out the maximum punishment on a convicted criminal or if you want to attempt to rehabilitate all the “bad” people. If you’re in the former camp, keeping someone alive in a prison is both cheaper for citizens and (I’d argue) a harsher punishment than death. If you’re in the latter camp, the death penalty precludes any opportunity to rehabilitate someone. It is just the final step in a cycle of violence that only reinforces the idea that killing is a reasonable way to solve problems.

Arguments like those from Hayden Daniel (under “What the right is saying”) that we could solve all this by bringing back the electric chair or firing squads might be convincing if the only goal is to “kill people more effectively than lethal injections.” Yet nearly 2% of all electric chair executions are botched, and since its inception it’s been one of the most gruesome tools for killing someone. Firing squads have a better track record of “working,” though they typically depend on trying to shoot the convicted’s heart — a target the shooters are known to miss. 

In reality, there’s no such thing as a guaranteed and humane execution — even when they work as intended, they’re gruesome. A long line of people have supported the death penalty until they’ve witnessed an execution, including by lethal injection, mostly because the notion that people just doze off and pass into another dimension at the command of the state is a complete farce. Executions have been going wrong since hangings and stonings, and they’ll continue to be botched into the future. Christa Pike’s wasn’t even the first botched execution in the U.S. this year. 

It wasn't even the first botched execution in Tennessee this year. 

It wasn’t even the first botched execution by this same doctor in Tennessee this year. 

A little bit of small-government libertarianism is all you actually need to oppose the death penalty. If you don’t trust the government to fix a pothole in your neighborhood, why do you think it can competently take the lives of human beings?

None of this requires any sympathy for Christa Pike. Her victim, Colleen Slemmer, would have just turned 51. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, remembers her daughter as a generous and kind person who volunteered at the Special Olympics, loved bowling and roller skating, and wanted to pursue a career in computers. Pike tortured her, then murdered her, then bragged about it later that night, telling someone she had “cut the victim’s throat six times, beaten her, and thrown asphalt at the victim’s head.” Pike relayed that Slemmer had begged her to stop, but she kept going because the victim continued to talk. She brought a piece of her skull to breakfast the next morning as a souvenir. Martinez is still alive — witnessing the events of the last few weeks — 31 years after her daughter’s murder, still trying to get justice. 

Again: Nobody needs to have any sympathy for Pike. But, not incidentally, I could easily argue that she was a bad candidate for the death penalty. On the moral spectrum of convicted killers, even those who committed gruesome murders, Pike is more sympathetic than most: She has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, she may have suffered brain damage in the womb, some evidence shows she was sexually and physically abused, and she was 18 years old at the time she committed the heinous murder — barely an adult (her boyfriend and accomplice was 17 and thus spared the death penalty). 

But I shouldn’t even have to make that argument. The real discussion we should be having is not whether a mentally ill killer needs to be kept alive in a hospital so the government can kill her. We should be talking about the death penalty itself, and the guaranteed preposterousness of situations like this that are all downstream of us accepting that the government can sometimes kill its citizens. We should end this uncivilized, immoral practice and find other ways to solve our problems.

Staff dissent.
Editor Audrey Moorehead and
Associate Editor Carina Pacheco
 
 
We agree that Tennessee’s botched execution attempt of Christa Pike is a horrible outcome, yet we take different lessons from it than Isaac does. Tennessee’s repeated failures with lethal injections should push us to re-examine how and when we implement the death penalty rather than discard the practice altogether.
 
Capital punishment does not need to deter crime or rehabilitate offenders to have merit; plainly, it should serve justice. Some crimes are so grave that state-sanctioned death is the only proportionate response. Many capital punishment defenders, us among them, agree that the modern process is too costly, drawn-out, and unfairly applied — and therefore far more dysfunctional and cruel than it needs to be. Consistent with the values of a speedy trial and an aversion to cruel, unusual punishment, the death penalty ought to be swiftly implemented in a fool-proof manner, reserved for the worst of the worst criminal offenses.
 
Much of the anti-death penalty argument rests on the fact that innocent people reside on death row, but that is a different issue worthy of far deeper probing: The law already requires certainty to convict, and we must meet that existing standard before approaching the death penalty question. At the same time, we should reserve capital punishment for a narrow, heinous set of crimes, such as mass shootings and serial or mass murder. This latest example in a string of failed executions is a prime opportunity to reevaluate how the death penalty is implemented to maximally serve justice when it’s due.

Take the survey: What do you think of the death penalty? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The Protect College Sports Act passes the Senate.
item.dc:creator: Ari Weitzman
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The Protect College Sports Act. On Monday, the Senate voted 77–22 to pass the Protect College Sports Act with support from 50 Republicans, 26 Democrats, and one independent. The bill would create a national regulatory framework for collegiate athletics and give the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) antitrust protection, allowing it to establish standards for student-athlete compensation, eligibility, transferring, and other activities. The House is expected to take up the bill after the November midterms. 

Back up: In June, Sens. Ted Cruz (R-TX), Maria Cantwell (D-WA), Eric Schmitt (R-MO), and Chris Coons (D-DE) introduced the bill in response to concerns about recent changes in college sports. In 2021, the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that the NCAA’s limits on certain education-related compensation for student-athletes violated antitrust law. The NCAA then implemented a name, image, and likeness (NIL) policy that allows student-athletes (and some high school athletes) to earn money without losing their eligibility. 

Initially, these payments could only come from third parties (such as advertisers), but in 2025, the rules were amended to allow NCAA Division I schools to compensate athletes directly. The policy has enabled some student-athletes — particularly football and basketball players — to earn millions in deals and led to more frequent transfers between schools. 

The Protect College Sports Act contains several provisions, including:

  • Codifying athletes’ ability to enter NIL deals
  • Creating reporting requirements for NIL compensation
  • Limiting the amount of money schools can spend on direct athlete payments 
  • Adding limited antitrust exemptions for the NCAA to implement rules on transferring and years of eligibility
  • Capping agent endorsement contract fees at 5%

The NCAA, major college athletic conferences, and President Donald Trump have come out in support of the bill, arguing that it will rein in “chaos” created by current NIL policies and establish a level playing field for college sports. “[The measure will] ensure student-athlete benefits are codified into federal law and future generations of young people can access those benefits and use college sports as the launching point for their careers,” NCAA President Charlie Baker said.

Labor groups, student-athlete organizations, and some Democrats have opposed the effort, saying it will strip athletes of newfound leverage and freedom. “This is a bill not about student-athletes, it’s about wealthy coaches and wealthy institutions and an NCAA who [have] enjoyed unbridled power for decades,” Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ) said. 

Today, we’ll share views from the right, left and sports writers on the bill, followed by Managing Editor Ari Weitzman’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right praise the bill for addressing problems in a flawed system.
  • Others argue that the law would benefit the colleges more than players.

The New York Post editorial board called the bill “a bipartisan win for protecting college sports.” 

“[The bill is] imperfect, but it has real promise to end the nonstop litigation and over-the-top bidding wars launched when the Supreme Court in 2021 tossed key NCAA rules on antitrust grounds,” the board wrote. “The old system had huge problems… But what followed was ruinous, with stars transferring to the highest bidder multiple times and schools stinting on women’s and Olympic sports as they chased talent that would bring in the most revenue. 

“The bill protects a collegian’s right to collect from the sale of his or her Name, Image and Likeness while setting national standards for transfers, eligibility, tampering and… limits on agents’ share of an athletes’ earnings,” the board said. “Yes, it gives the NCAA a partial antitrust exemption so it can’t get sued for enforcing eligibility and transfer limits and lets it limit coaches’ job-hopping rights, too — but keeping college sports different from the pros has to start somewhere.”

In The Tennessean, Cameron Smith said the “Protect College Sports Act favors universities over players.”

“Billed as a necessary measure to bring order to the chaotic landscape of name, image and likeness (NIL) agreements, the bill is touted as a rescue mission for a beloved American tradition,” Smith wrote. “In reality, it represents something far more familiar inside the Beltway: powerful institutions using federal authority to secure special treatment… The true engine of the bill is its conditional antitrust exemption.”

“Under the guise of protecting amateurism, Congress is offering the collegiate sports establishment a legal carve-out to sidestep the laws of supply and demand to avoid sharing its eye-popping profits with the athletes producing the value on the field,” Smith said. “Transforming college athletes into recognized employees who collectively bargain with leagues and universities is not a threat to college sports; it is an equitable solution.”

What the left is saying.
  • Some on the left say the proposed law solely protects NCAA interests.
  • Others recognize some benefits but ultimately see the bill as a loss for athletes.

In The New Republic, Matt Ford argued the bill “will only protect the NCAA’s billions.”

“College athletes were finally able to pursue fair-market compensation for their services over the last few years thanks to a series of major court rulings. Now the NCAA and its allies are trying to turn back the clock to keep as much of the money that college athletes generate as possible,” Ford wrote. “Every good thing in the PCSA is a sweetener designed to make its real purpose easier to swallow.”

“The PCSA gives the NCAA immunity from federal antitrust laws when it enforces rules on compensation, transfers, broadcast rights, and more among member schools and conferences. Federal antitrust laws have been a powerful tool for college athletes to keep at least some of the wealth that they generate for themselves. With the PCSA, Congress would slam that door shut,” Ford said. “The good news is that the PCSA might not become law in the 119th Congress.”

In The Free Press, Joe Nocera wrote “last night, college athletes lost.”

“[The bill] does some good things. It gives players a 10-year window to graduate from the school they played for. It limits players to one transfer, which even I concede is necessary. It requires universities to give its athletes comprehensive healthcare benefits,” Nocera said. “But it does absolutely nothing to curb coaches’ pay, or the millions spent on fancy facilities, or any of the other things that have caused college athletics to become so outrageously expensive. 

“Except one: It sets a cap on the amount of money an athletic department can spend on its athletes — not just football players but athletes in every sport,” Nocera wrote. “That amount is $21.6 million. (There is an additional $22.5 million ‘retention fund’ that is supposed to be used to keep star players from transferring.) That’s not nothing, of course, but it means that unlike most Americans, college athletes will once again be deprived of their chance to cash in on their prowess."

What sports writers are saying.
  • Some sports writers applaud the bill for protecting athletes.
  • Others lament how the proposed law might bail out bad coaches.

In Sportico, Lamell J. McMorris suggested “student-athletes need protection.”

“The agent world around these young athletes is largely unregulated, and too much of it preys on the very kids it claims to serve. [The business] is not built around the best interests of student-athletes, and this bill finally brings order to it,” McMorris wrote. “It protects Olympic and nonrevenue sports, invests in women’s athletics, strengthens health and safety, safeguards scholarships, and creates real accountability for schools and athletes alike.”

“I do not dismiss the people opposing this bill,” McMorris said. “[One objection] is that collective bargaining should fix all of this. I wish it were that simple. More than 80% of Division I schools are public institutions, and their athletes would be state employees, outside the reach of federal labor law and, in many states, barred from bargaining at all… Meanwhile, the protections in this bill are real, and they are available now.”

In USA Today, Blake Toppmeyer wrote “bad college football coaches have it good with Protect College Sports Act.”

“Perhaps the biggest winner in the ‘Protect College Sports Act’ passed by the Senate? Losing college football coaches,” Toppmeyer said. “This bill, which politicians pretend will address the ‘chaos’ and ‘crisis’ inside college athletics, fails to address the soaring salaries for coaches and their bosses, or the $50 million severance checks for fired coaches… There’s never been a better time to be a bad football coach. 

“Just ask South Carolina’s Shane Beamer. He’s making $8.25 million this season, and he’s 2-11 in his past 13 games against Power Four opponents,” Toppmeyer wrote. “I don’t actually believe Congress should regulate coaches’ salaries or buyouts, either. Instead, force university presidents and chancellors to do their jobs. If schools can’t pay the athletics bills, then make them rein in spending and stop the contract stupidity, instead of awarding them a bailout.”

My take.
Ari Weitzman
Managing Editor
 
 
  • Most college sports don’t have huge issues, but the biggest money-makers have descended into complete disorder. 
  • The new status quo risks eroding what makes college sports appealing. 
  • This bill is imperfect, but it gets the important stuff right.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

As I mentioned at the start of today’s edition, I ran track (for one year) in college. Balancing school, sports and work can be really difficult, but it can also be really fun; and for most students competing in college sports at the level I was, the model isn’t broken.

However, for the most visible sports, particularly football and basketball, the operational model is fundamentally flawed. 

First, the collegiate sports landscape is simply chaotic. Decades ago, college conferences were neatly organized by geography. Today, Texas and Oklahoma play in the Southeastern Conference while the Atlantic Coast Conference is home to Stanford and Cal-Berkeley. The formerly Midwestern Big Ten stretches from Rutgers to the University of Southern California (USC). Meanwhile, the Pac-10 (excuse me, Pac-12) was whittled down to two teams and now is limping along with nine. Smaller conferences wither away while mega-conferences demand cross-country travel for their teams, making a total farce of the idea that athletes are “students first” — how is anyone supposed to keep up with classes while flying from Los Angeles to New Jersey for an in-conference game?

The obvious reason for this convoluted setup is the second problem in college sports: money. USC is in the Big Ten simply because the school knows it can make more money through TV deals if it’s in a conference with better teams. Smaller conferences have no leverage for keeping their teams from leaving, and the major schools and major conferences have started concentrating resources at the expense of smaller conferences, smaller schools, and the academic schedules of the players themselves. 

Speaking of the players, for a long time, the NCAA operated a business model that sounds downright criminal: It sold a billion-dollar product without paying the people who made it. Not only were student-athletes forbidden from taking any kind of compensation (lest it sully the sanctity of their scholarship at their chosen university), but the NCAA — already collecting over a billion dollars in television rights, advertising deals, and licensing fees — could profit from these athletes’ name, image, and likeness (NIL) without them earning a dime. 

These rules led to absurdities. Several football players at the University of Oklahoma had to pay $3.83 in fines for having illegally large portions of pasta at a graduation dinner. Former NFL star Arian Foster admitted he colluded with the University of Tennessee’s coaches to take illicit tacos from them, all so he could have enough food to perform suitably for Neyland Stadium’s 100,000+ spectators. 

Thus, problem three was born: NIL madness. The NCAA allowed athletes to take NIL deals to profit from sponsorships or having their likeness used for promotions. In theory, this is a good thing. Finally, some fairness for the college athletes who put their bodies on the line for the product and had to scrimp for enough food to eat while NCAA executives (and, for the big teams, their coaches) raked in the money. But the new NIL rules tilted the balance towards star players, allowing them to transfer out for more lucrative payouts (or better playing opportunities) elsewhere. Thus, the people the entire business model of college sports really depends on — the fans — were made to suffer, as they could watch their program develop a special athlete and then watch that athlete walk away to greener pastures. 

The degradation of the fan relationship is one of the biggest risks of the current chaos, which I don’t think enough people are talking about. College fans are incredibly loyal to their schools, and that loyalty is the base of the intercollegiate sports megabusiness. If the Mississippi States of the world become feeder programs for major schools, if the field tilts more and more against the underdog, if Kansas is forced to play a home game in London, then that base of support could erode and the whole house of cards could come crashing down.

The intractable problem the Protect College Sports Act faces is the need to provide some stability to this mess, all without infringing on the collective rights of student-athletes and while protecting the athletes in small-market sports.

The bill takes the problem in parts, and in the collegiate spirit, I’ll grade how effective I think the major elements of this potential law will be.

Antitrust exception for the NCAA: A. Nearly every core rule of the NCAA could be a violation of the Sherman Act, which forbids an organization like the NCAA from limiting whom competing businesses can hire and how much they can pay them. Sports teams composed of students are not the same as most businesses, and collegiate sports’ regulatory body needs more ability to regulate its teams. Under this bill, the NCAA can set rules on transfers, eligibility, and recruiting in a way that should provide more structure.

Athletes’ rights: A. This is the necessary counterpart to giving the NCAA more power to regulate. If this act is passed, athletes will have a federally protected right to receive NIL money, scholarships, and protections for their health and safety. The law would also cap agent fees at 5% and ensure the ability of schools to pay their students directly. No more insiders fleecing unwitting 18-year-olds, and permanently gone will be the days of star running backs relying on back-door tacos.

Transfer and eligibility caps: B-. The counterpart to the counterpart, this would create a federal law, not an NCAA regulation, that limits college eligibility to five years and student-athletes to one transfer within those five years. Without this in place, star players could be in a constant state of free agency and more prone to pause their eligibility. If the NCAA gets an antitrust exception, then the government has to give itself some power here. But it’s hard not to feel a little queasy about potential government overreach. My biggest concerns are what happens when a student wants to transfer for non-opportunistic reasons; I could easily see this regulation being overly burdensome to many athletes. Still, the presence of a guardrail is sensible to me, especially given the widespread abuses of the current eligibility system.

Women’s and Olympic sports protections: A. One of the concerns with colleges and Congress getting more authority over regulating sports is that the for-profit model might shoulder out athletic opportunities for the bus-riders like I was in college. This provision requires schools to keep as many non-revenue athletes as they had in the 2024-2025 academic year, which I think is a tidy and clever way of applying that protection. It also requires schools that pool their media rights to redistribute some of their money to other teams, which is a way of preventing football teams from building palatial facilities while other teams get table scraps.

Conference rules: C. As hinted at in the previous bullet, this provision allows schools to pool and negotiate their media rights (an amendment to the 1961 Sports Broadcasting Act). This would allow conferences to spread their profits to smaller schools and conferences in a similar way as the NFL does now with their smaller markets, which will give these programs similar leverage to the megaconferences (and which is why the SEC and Big Ten oppose this portion of the bill). I’m very supportive of this collective bargaining among teams, but I’m not convinced this will meaningfully level a playing field that’s already so tilted. The act tries to address the power agglomeration among the big conferences by capping the number of teams per conference at 20, but that number is frankly far too high. The bill prevents the worst case of college sports becoming just two conferences, sure, but it doesn’t really address the problem as it exists today.

At the end of the day, I think this is a good law whose time has come. It’s not perfect, but it’ll be an improvement. And in an era where Congress can scarcely be asked to do more than the bare minimum, I’m happy to see lawmakers get together to act to try to tackle a problem in a bipartisan fashion. I’d love it if our lawmakers could bring that same spirit to balancing our budget, but that’s a problem for another day.

Take the survey: What do you think of the bill? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The ACA cancelations.
item.dc:creator: Will Kaback
item.description: Plus, what’s going on with the Trump administration’s new PSAs?
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The ACA cancelations. Last Tuesday, September 22, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) said it had canceled healthcare enrollments for roughly 760,000 people under the Affordable Care Act (ACA) due to alleged fraud or improper documentation. In a press briefing announcing the cancelations, Vice President JD Vance and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said that Covid-era subsidies and relaxed verification under President Joe Biden led to rampant abuse of the federally regulated ACA marketplace. The vice president’s White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud estimates the enforcement action will save $2.2 billion in taxpayer-funded subsidies.

Back up: In 2010, President Barack Obama signed the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (also known as “Obamacare”) into law. The ACA increased coverage and expanded Medicaid benefits for more people through government-regulated markets. In 2021, during President Joe Biden’s administration, Congress passed the American Rescue Plan, which offered premium subsidies and tax credits for those enrolling in the ACA. Then in 2022, Congress extended the enhanced subsidies through 2025 with the Inflation Reduction Act. Congress allowed those subsidies to expire at the end of 2025.  

ACA enrollment increased from 11 million to 24 million people under the Biden administration. Oz alleged in March that as many as 5 million enrollees receive ACA benefits and subsidies fraudulently. Just over 19 million people received benefits through the federally managed exchange as of June 2026, meaning the enforcement action targeted roughly 4% of enrollees. 

Those culled from the program were enrolled through third-party brokers, had zero-premium plans and lacked verifiable Social Security numbers or immigration status documents, leading the anti-fraud task force to suspect the beneficiaries were fraudulent. “We call them phantoms, because we believe most of them don’t exist or they had no idea they had coverage,” Oz said. Vice President Vance identified the role of brokers, who receive a payment for enrolling people in ACA programs, as key to the problem. “On the one hand, brokers are paid money to feed patients into the system, while on the other hand, the government isn’t even checking whether the people enrolled are actually eligible for the program,” Vance said.

Critics of the move argue that CMS cast too wide a net and could be removing coverage for many legitimate cases. “There is widespread agreement that unauthorized enrollments should be canceled,” Cynthia Cox, ACA researcher at health policy center KFF, said. “The question is whether these were all indeed unauthorized enrollments and whether this was the appropriate process for determining whether an enrollee was legitimate or not.”

Below, we’ll cover what the left and right are saying about the ACA cancelations, then Senior Editor Will Kaback gives his take.

What the left is saying.
  • The left criticizes the cancelations, with some saying they will hurt the healthcare system.
  • Some say Vance’s anti-fraud task force shares flaws with DOGE.
  • Others recognize the need to address fraud but say this action ignores underlying issues.

In The Guardian, Melody Schreiber said “Trump is threatening the entire US health system.”

“No details were provided about how many enrollees were fictional, enrolled by fraudulent brokers without their knowledge, or expelled because of income restrictions,” Schreiber wrote. “The people were identified by three factors: they’d been enrolled by a broker or agent, had all of their ACA premium paid by the tax credit, and they had not supplied Social Security numbers or immigration documents.” 

“About 35% of ACA enrollees have never used their health insurance, [said Medicare and Medicaid Administrator Mehmet Oz],” Schreiber said. “But it’s not unusual for healthy people to be enrolled in insurance and not need to use it, [according to public policy researcher Edwin Park]… By removing lower-risk enrollees, insurance premiums could increase or insurers could decide to leave markets entirely, he said… When people lose their health insurance, it has ripple effects — including added pressure on health systems that affect all patients.”

In MS NOW, Steve Benen wrote about what “Vance’s task force has in common with Musk’s DOGE gambit.”

“Independent estimates show billions of dollars are lost every year to fraud and abuse. If the vice president believes he can help address the problem, more power to him,” Benen said. “The trouble is, Vance claims he has already made extraordinary headway in uncovering fraud — to the tune of more than $260 billion — but those boasts aren’t standing up well to scrutiny. If this sounds at all familiar, it’s because a similar story unfolded last year.

“Elon Musk was put in charge of… DOGE, and it too created an online resource that purported to show all of the billions of dollars the endeavor was saving American taxpayers,” Benen wrote. “To be sure, the underlying point of these resources sounds great… The trouble is, both initiatives seemed wholly unprepared for what might happen when people who know what they’re talking about bothered to review their work.”

In MS NOW, Miranda Yaver suggested “a heavy dose of skepticism.” 

“The first Trump administration helped empower the very brokers it now claims are fraudulently enrolling people,” Yaver wrote. “While the second Trump administration is taking aim at perverse incentives that may have arisen, sweeping disenrollments ignore the failures of policy design. That is, when the previous Trump administration gave brokers more power as intermediaries… the government failed to build a regulatory regime that would police their behavior.”

“CMS’s decision to impose a moratorium on new agents and brokers may prove to be a Band-Aid solution,” Yaver said. “An appropriate response would not just penalize actors who are in the wrong (such as this) but also impose greater regulatory protection to prevent this in the future. The Trump administration, ideologically inclined against consumer protection, has largely opted for piecemeal responses… while leaving systemic failures in place.”

What the right is saying.
  • The right supports the cuts, with many saying the administration is effectively fighting fraud.
  • Some argue that this effort should have bipartisan support.
  • Others push back on Democrats’ characterizations of the cancelations.

In The Federalist, Chris Bray said the administration is “doing normal anti-fraud work with increased focus.”

“Federal regulations that were first written during the Obama administration in 2012 explicitly describe the process by which fraudulent Obamacare enrollments can be terminated by government officials, and here’s the funny part: Every administration does this. The termination of fraudulent Obamacare enrollments is a normal CMS activity,” Bray wrote. “The Biden administration routinely announced the termination of fraudulent Obamacare enrollments.”

“By the standard Democrats are applying this week, cruel Joe Biden viciously stripped healthcare coverage from tens of thousands of Americans,” Bray said. “But not really, because the whole fake panic is completely made-up and stupid. The Trump administration is doing normal anti-fraud work with increased focus and seriousness, which is only a scandal if you’re dumb enough to be elected to Congress as a Democrat.”

The Las Vegas Review-Journal editorial board suggested fraud “shouldn’t be a partisan issue.” 

“Just because a government agency allocates money for a noble-sounding cause doesn’t mean the money is well spent. Elected officials and government employees have a duty to ensure that taxpayer money is spent carefully,” the board said. “Politicians from both parties talk about the need to eliminate ‘waste, fraud and abuse.’ But notice the reaction to the Trump administration’s efforts to actually do just that.”

“The DOJ alleges that ‘more than $10 million intended to help low-income families pay for childcare was instead funneled to bogus daycare providers,’” the board wrote. “Yes, this White House has a tendency to exaggerate for political purposes. But fraud against the taxpayers is a serious problem… Democrats should work with the Trump administration to root out fraud, not attack Mr. Trump and Mr. Vance when they work to do so.”

The Washington Post editorial board argued “JD Vance is not ripping away anyone’s health insurance coverage.”

“Former House speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-CA) wrote on social media that ‘using the false pretext of fighting fraud to strip Americans of their healthcare is as cynical as it is cruel.’ Except that’s not what’s happening,” the board wrote. “Even if the account met all of [the] requirements [for removal], the insurer was still required to reach out to the individual via two forms of communication. Only when insurers received no response after 30 days was the account removed, according to CMS.” 

“Fraud grew rampant in recent years because the Biden administration increased Obamacare enrollment by expanding eligibility for zero-premium plans while failing to perform sufficient due diligence,” the board said. “Money given to scammers is money that doesn’t help needy people receive health care. Democrats should wholeheartedly support throwing the book at these criminals. Downplaying the scale of abuse undermines public confidence in the safety net.”

My take.
Will Kaback
Senior Editor
 
 
  • Defrauding insurers on the federal marketplace is a protracted problem that predates Trump.
  • CMS’s actions here are justified, and I think the methods they used were reasonable.
  • I harbor reservations about Vance’s broader anti-fraud initiative and the administration’s track record, but this effort looks like a win.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

“Trump Officials Eject 750,000 From Obamacare Markets, Claiming Fraud,” is one of those headlines that rolls down the conveyor belt of daily news items and snatches your attention, particularly if you or a loved one are enrolled in a government healthcare plan. It’s also a story that could create more confusion than clarity. So let’s nail down a few key points up front.

All enrollees whose coverage was canceled received their health insurance through the federally facilitated Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace — HealthCare.gov — so those insured through state-based exchanges weren’t affected. Neither were those who signed up for a plan on their own. Vice President Vance’s task force only looked into enrollments mediated by agents or brokers, who serve as middlemen between the government, insurance companies, and individuals. 

In theory, brokers have a useful role: They identify people eligible for ACA benefits and help them get health insurance (they’re then paid on commission by insurers). But these agents have also become a burgeoning source of fraud. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) found that first-time brokers who registered for the 2026 plan year were disproportionately responsible for enrollment activity flagged as high-risk or fraudulent, including missing Social Security Numbers, unverifiable citizenship status, and unresolved income verification. 

Those discrepancies may be explainable, but unverified information like that is an alarm bell that brokers may be enrolling people without their knowledge and lying about their income so they qualify for a $0 premium (and thus wouldn’t know they had been signed up). Or they could be switching people to a different plan without their knowledge to collect a new commission. Or they could be fudging personal data to make someone eligible who shouldn’t have been. Concerns over this behavior are bipartisan: In 2024, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) called on CMS to take urgent action to address brokers fraudulently enrolling people in ACA plans. 

Beyond bad broker behavior, other areas of the HealthCare.gov marketplace have become hotspots for fraud. In 2024, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) tested whether four made-up applicants could get approved for coverage — all four were accepted, at a total cost of $2,350 per month. For 2025, it created 20 fake applicants, and 18 were still receiving coverage nine months into the plan year, at a cost of over $10,000 per month. GAO also found 30,000 applications in plan year 2023 and 160,000 applications in plan year 2024 that had “likely unauthorized changes by agents or brokers.”

Separately, the Congressional Budget Office informed lawmakers in August 2025 that an estimated 2.3 million enrollees intentionally misrepresented their income to qualify for ACA tax credits in 2025, up from an estimated 1.3 million in 2023. And the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation reported in June that nearly half of ACA enrollment growth between 2021 and 2024 was “suspected to be improper, phantom, or fraudulent.” 

Considering the range and scope of these findings, it feels pretty disingenuous for Democratic politicians like Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Nancy Pelosi to suggest that the Trump administration is villainously trying to rip health insurance away from hundreds of thousands of people for no apparent reason. Some people may have been mistakenly caught up in this probe, but we don’t have enough information to say that yet (and one week after this announcement, I haven’t seen any reports of people claiming they were wrongly kicked off their plan). Based on what we know right now, I think this effort was both justified and properly executed. 

When I reviewed criticisms from the left about the cancelations, I noticed the arguments were mostly based on suspicion of any fraud-related initiatives from the Trump administration. Take the three pieces we chose for today’s edition. In MS NOW, Miranda Yaver wrote, “Given the administration’s track record, there are reasons to view this announcement with a heavy dose of skepticism.” Also in MS NOW, Steve Benen alluded to “ample reason for skepticism” about Vance’s fraud task force. And The Guardian’s Melody Schreiber dedicated the bulk of her piece to quoting experts who suggested ill intent by Vance and co. 

What also struck me, though, was that these articles didn’t offer evidence that the enrollments were improperly canceled — just that CMS may have made some mistakes, and the Trump administration doesn’t deserve the benefit of the doubt. 

I think both those points have some credence, especially when the administration has misled the public about so many other “anti-fraud” initiatives. As Isaac documented in his retrospective on DOGE last month, Elon Musk’s ill-fated effort enacted sweeping cuts with no apparent strategy, lied about its savings, and likely cost taxpayers billions. Vance’s fraud task force has also made dubious claims; the vice president has said his group has found roughly $250 billion in fraud, but they haven’t shared the basis for that number publicly (a New York Times analysis found that Vance included cases that were identified and prosecuted under the Biden administration). 

Vance and CMS could have headed off this skepticism by offering more detail about those who were kicked off their plans. Specifically, knowing what proportion of the cancelations were for suspected broker fraud, ineligibility, or improper documentation would give a clearer idea of where the biggest areas of concern exist. 

However, acknowledging those points doesn’t invalidate this anti-fraud initiative. Remember, the affected enrollments met four criteria: They lacked a valid Social Security or immigration identification number, had 100% of their premium covered by tax credits, hadn’t used their coverage since it was activated, and had never made contact with the insurer. To me, that’s a sharp approach to rooting out the areas of concern for fraud. Even after all four boxes were checked, the insurer of the suspicious plan still had to reach out to the enrollee through two different forms of communication and give them 30 days to respond before the government canceled their coverage, providing ample opportunity to correct a mistake. And if their plan was canceled improperly, individuals can still re-enroll. 

I don’t blame anyone whose eyebrow twitched when they first read about the ACA cancelations. I had the same reaction. But knowing the scale of the issues that have long existed in the ACA marketplace, I’m glad the administration took action, and I think the criteria it used were sound. Am I still skeptical of how the White House is addressing purported fraud in other areas of government? Absolutely. Do I think Vance’s task force is scrutinizing Obamacare with entirely pure intentions? I don’t. But I can hold those reservations and still find this effort necessary and valid. 

Take the survey: Do you support this action? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The 2026 midterms preview.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, a hacking incident at the FBI.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The 2026 midterm elections. Tuesday marks 35 days until federal elections will be held for all 435 U.S. House seats and 35 of the 100 U.S. Senate seats. Additionally, 36 states will elect governors and 46 states will vote on a total of 6,139 state legislators. Currently, most election models heavily favor Democrats to take back the House and give the party a slight edge to flip the Senate.

Back up: Republicans have a 53–47 majority in the Senate, counting independents who caucus with Democrats, so Democrats must pick up four seats to take control of Congress’s upper chamber (accounting for Vice President JD Vance’s potential tie-breaking vote). Republicans have a 218–214 advantage in the House, with one independent (Californian Rep. Kevin Kiley, a former Republican) and two vacancies. Democrats will need to control 218 seats to win a majority. 

Sabato’s Crystal Ball, which analyzes races according to factors like election history and polling, favors Democrats to hold 48 Senate seats after the midterms and Republicans to hold 47, with Alaska, Iowa, Ohio, Maine, and Texas considered tossups. Sabato describes three seats as “lean Democrat”: the Republican-held North Carolina and Democrat-held seats in Michigan and New Hampshire. The Senate race in Kansas is the only one considered “lean Republican.” In the House, the GOP is favored in 203 races, compared to Democrats in 211; the remaining 21 House elections are tossups. 

Democrats have campaigned against President Donald Trump’s policies, highlighting healthcare cuts from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), inflation, and the war in Iran. “Democrats are focused on the American people’s priorities,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (NY) said. “Lowering costs, bringing stability, and fighting back against this administration’s rampant, rampant corruption.”

Republicans have promoted the OBBBA’s tax cuts and argued that Democratic candidates are too aligned with the party’s ascendant far left. They have also centered immigration policies and social issues. “As we summarize [the election],” Speaker Mike Johnson (LA) said, “it’s a contrast between common sense and crazy, and now common sense and communism.”

Below are views from the right and left on the outlook for the midterms with one month to go. Then, Executive Editor Isaac Saul shares his take.

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right expect Republicans to outperform current expectations. 
  • Others say that much remains uncertain about the eventual results.
  • Still others suggest that Republicans are headed for losses in both chambers.

In the New York Sun, Lawrence Kudlow argued “nobody should underestimate Trump and the GOP.”

“While the Republicans are running some really solid candidates… the Democrats are running these far-left wing socialists like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, [James] Talarico in Texas, and far-left Troy Jackson in Maine. It’s really the mirror image of Republican mistakes in 2022,” Kudlow wrote. “And although gasoline prices are high, and that’s an issue, it’s also true they’re almost identical to gas prices under President Biden.”

“Not downplaying the gas issue, but there’s a lot of other very good things going on in Mr. Trump’s economy. Private jobs are up by a million since he was re-elected. Federal jobs have declined by about 350,000. The economy is being restructured away from big-government socialism,” Kudlow said. “Voters want common sense, not crazy values. And that’s why… nobody should underestimate Mr. Trump and the GOP.”

In the Wall Street Journal, Karl Rove said “this election season will likely have more surprises than most.”

“What if much of what we think we know about the midterms is wrong?... Democrats lead the generic ballot, 50.4% to 41.8%, in the RealClearPolitics average,” Rove wrote. “But what if, at least in the House, that’s too broad a measure for the races that matter most? A Sept. 17 Cook Political Report poll says the Democratic advantage across the 37 battleground districts is 2 points… That could mean a smaller pickup than they expect.”

“Republicans have a record of success to run on: closing the border, keeping Americans from a record tax hike by passing the Big Beautiful Bill, and virtually ending peak wokeism by attacking DEI in all its forms. But what if voters are more concerned with problems they face now?” Rove asked. “I have my hunches about what will happen. So do you. But what’s conventional wisdom today could look like folly six weeks from now.”

In National Review, Jeffrey Blehar wrote about “preparing for the worst in the Senate elections.”

“The GOP is playing defense in so many states it has come to think of as home turf that it’s easy to forget how many opportunities for his party to make gains were squandered by Trump in pursuit of his private grudges and obsessions,” Blehar said. “The GOP is virtually guaranteed to lose at least one Senate seat it currently holds: Facing threats from Trump that he would back a primary challenger, North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis dropped his race for reelection.”

“The one potential pickup opportunity that exists for Republicans is in Michigan… Several factors militate against optimism, however. The state’s DNA is fundamentally Democratic; it has not elected a Republican to the Senate since 1994,” Blehar wrote. “With so many Senate races so close… only a brave man or a fool would attempt to predict the final result… But a red harvest is likely approaching, a bloody cull, and Trump now seems to be preparing for the worst.”

What the left is saying.
  • Many on the left note ominous signs in every direction for the GOP.
  • Some suggest that Republicans’ fundraising advantage won’t save them.
  • Others say GOP candidates are distancing themselves from Trump too late.

In CNN, Aaron Blake said “[this] could be the worst midterm for the GOP this century.”

“The Republican Party’s two worst midterm elections in the 21st Century were in 2006 and 2018… The president’s continued decline has now made him clearly a more unpopular president than he was in 2018 and Bush was in 2006 — at least on a national scale,” Blake wrote. “Today the Iran war is more unpopular than Iraq was… There is a real question whether Iran is as big an issue as Iraq was, given that unlike in Iraq, there aren’t boots on the ground.” 

“But similar numbers called the wars ‘extremely important’ to their vote in 2006 (46%) and today (48%),” Blake said. “There is one very important measurement that hasn’t tipped towards Democrats as much as they’d like — at least not yet. And that’s the generic ballot… For now, every other major measure appears to be very bad for Trump and the GOP. So it’s worth watching to see whether this one follows suit.”

In MS NOW, Hayes Brown suggested that GOP spending won’t “persuade voters to ignore their own economic pain.”

“The extra money to buy ads notwithstanding, there is little in the record for congressional Republicans to promote,” Brown wrote. “While many of the harshest cuts to the social safety net used to pay for its tax cuts were punted until next year or later, hundreds of thousands of Americans have already seen their benefits slashed in a bad economic environment — and know exactly which party to blame. 

“When they don’t have a positive message, campaigns often blanket media markets with negative messaging,” Brown said. “Major Republican bogeymen for this campaign season have included the twin specters of communism and socialism, or, as a talking point Vice President JD Vance and numerous others have repeated goes: ‘common sense versus crazy.’... But while the GOP’s life raft of cash might save some candidates, there’s not enough room for everyone to climb aboard.”

In The American Prospect, David Dayen called Republican candidates’ distancing from Trump “performative and inauthentic.”

“After a notable absence, an anti-war movement has emerged to finally challenge a president over the unpopular conflict in Iran. Not in the streets so much, but in ads and statements from Republicans trying to salvage their doomed election campaigns,” Dayen wrote. “This shift is almost 700 days late and about $3 trillion short. For 99.9% of the past two years, Republicans have fallen in line with every insane maneuver and utterance from this administration.”

“Since January 20, 2025, the Republican Congress could have stopped the imposition of tariffs through existing mechanisms.
