They could have cut off funding for wars they don’t like,” Dayen said. “They could have impeached and removed him from office, with Democratic support. Instead they support Trump’s every whim in almost perfect lockstep, no matter how crazy. These deathbed conversions are preposterous, and everybody knows it.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • One way to look at the midterms is that Republicans are cruising for disaster, especially without Trump on the ballot to energize his base.
  • However, Democrats could easily underperform polls in the same way Republicans did in 2022.
  • I’m going to resist a prediction for now, since a lot can change in a month.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Heading into the 2022 midterms, Republicans were poised to ride a red wave and take complete control of Congress from Democrats. 

The equation was simple. The Senate was split 50–50, and Democrats had a narrow advantage in the House. From 1934–2018, the party in the White House had lost an average of 28 House seats and four Senate seats in midterm elections. President Biden’s approval ratings were bad, inflation was pummeling economic sentiment, and the president faced mounting criticism of his handling of the Russia–Ukraine war. Meanwhile, Republicans had a polling advantage over Democrats, and a consensus quickly formed that they were poised to have a big night.

Sound familiar?

We know what happened instead: Democrats handed in a shocking midterm performance for an incumbent party, holding the Senate and keeping the race for the House so competitive it took days to call. Cook Political Report’s Dave Wasserman called it “the craziest Election Night I’ve ever seen.” I could only find one reputable analyst in the entire country who predicted that outcome: a Democratic strategist named Simon Rosenberg. I was prudent enough to cite Rosenberg in our last newsletter before the midterms, calling him out as a dissenting voice worth considering.

Everyone who predicted a red wave, including me, was wrong.

Of course, four years have passed since that midterm outcome, which is plenty of time for everyone to stack their hubris and bury the memory of their wrongness. I’ll try not to make that mistake here.

I see two ways to frame those 2022 midterm results now, and they invite nearly opposite predictions about what’s going to happen in November. One framing is that the 2022 midterms were a good example of Republicans’ weakness when Trump is not on the ballot. The party had an opportunity for huge electoral gains, but it couldn’t turn out enough voters without their leader on the ballot, its candidates lacked enthusiasm, and the red wave was more like a middling tide. This is the downside of building a movement around a single man. It’s also possible things in 2022 just weren’t that bad, so Democrats did better than people thought (especially with the motivating factor of Roe v. Wade being overturned). This time, voter sentiment is definitively worse about Trump, Republicans, and the economy. 

In this frame, 2026 could be an even bigger blue wave year than any of us are expecting. Trump is in office, yes, but since he isn’t on the ballot, his base might not show up. Not only that, but the president has historically bad midterm approval numbers, Republicans are in power, and Republicans are the ones losing on the generic ballot. That could spell disaster.

The second frame is almost the opposite: Polling gives us some information, but it’s not a sure thing. Forecasting is even less reliable. Polls have missed badly in the special elections over the last few months. Much is being made of Trump’s deteriorating polling numbers, but Democrats still have an even bigger problem: Their party and their policies are also historically unpopular. Lastly, a lot of ink has been spilled about all the Trump voters who regret casting a ballot for him or the former allies who are jumping ship or the Republicans who are scrubbing him from their websites — so much so that it could be creating a false impression of the electorate. Trump wasn’t on the ballot in 2018, either, but he was in the White House; and despite his unpopularity, Republicans expanded their Senate majority while losing the House — a pretty mixed outcome. 

Anecdotally, if I could describe the mood among my Trump-supporting friends and family, I’d describe it less as “they are abandoning Trump” and more as “they are feeling let down by Trump.” They aren’t thrilled with the president or the economy or the war, but they’d still vote for him over a generic Democrat nine times out of ten. It’s hard to know precisely how widespread that sentiment is — that’s what the election is for. 

In this second frame, it isn’t hard to throw several grains of salt on the polls, consider my own pop-up focus groups, and see Republicans narrowly losing the House but holding onto the Senate (or even expanding their majority). That would leave us talking about the “blue wave” that never was in the same way we spoke about 2022’s undelivered red wave.

If that’s what happens, the midterms could still be a win for Democrats because they would have taken back the House. That alone would be enough to grind the Trump presidency to a crawl and launch a dozen investigations into senior ranking members of his administration. That we are even discussing the possibility of Democrats winning the Senate is rather remarkable. Much like “red wave” prognostication was everywhere in 2022, we’ve endured think piece after think piece after think piece for the past eight years explaining how Democrats may never win the Senate again because of the institutional advantages Republicans enjoy. Now, in the first election since many of those pieces were published, they have a very realistic path to doing just that.

The races I’m most keen to watch are taking place in Virginia, Iowa, and Texas. Virginia’s Second Congressional District will be a great testing ground for theories about how important the Iran war is to voters. Jen Kiggans, a Republican incumbent, is defending the seat against Elaine Luria, a Democrat. Both Kiggans and Luria are Navy veterans. Their district has some of the highest numbers of active-duty troops and veterans in the country, and Kiggans won the seat by beating Luria in 2022. Kiggans has repeatedly voted down resolutions to limit Trump’s war powers while Luria has made opposition to the war central to her campaign. Early voting in Virginia’s second will provide a signal of how motivating an issue the war is to voters.

In Iowa, Democratic state auditor Rob Sand is running a unique campaign for governor against Republican businessman Zach Lahn. Sand is a moderate Democrat’s dream: allergic to any culture war debates, willing to speak from the center, and relentlessly focused on pragmatic government and attacking corruption. Iowa has been reliably red for a decade, but both Sand and Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek have a real shot this year. If they put in strong numbers — or even turn Iowa blue — Republicans are in for a bad night.

Finally, and fittingly, we turn to Texas for the big one: James Talarico vs. Ken Paxton, in which Democrats test how progressive a candidate can be and still win in Texas, while Republicans test how corrupt a candidate can be and still win in Texas. But more interesting stuff is happening further down the ballot. As part of the gerrymandering war Trump launched in 2025, Texas redrew its congressional maps to gain as many as five seats for the GOP. Winning those seats, though, relies heavily on keeping Trump’s advantages with Latino voters across South Texas. 

That plan will be tested in Texas’s 15th and 35th Congressional Districts, where Latino voters are an outsized share of the electorate. If Republicans lose some of the voters they won over in previous elections, they’ll also lose congressional seats in these heavily Latino districts where margins are dangerously narrow. I could even see a world where we reflect on these gerrymandering efforts as a strategic error, putting otherwise reliable GOP seats in play by stretching their advantages too thin.

With five weeks to go until election day, I’ll close with this: A lot can happen in a month. For now, some kind of blue wave looks likely, and early voting has already begun — meaning voter sentiment today will impact the outcome. But I’ve seen how quickly things can change in just a few days, let alone a few weeks, so I’ll be keeping my eyes and ears open as we barrel toward Election Day.

Last week, a hacking group called ShinyHunters said it had accessed a large amount of data containing personal information about Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) employees and applicants. FBI leaders have acknowledged the hack and told employees that their information may have been stolen, asking them to report unsolicited contacts or threats. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters has demanded the bureau take down a posted advisory about the group by the end of the day on Tuesday or risk the release of the stolen information (though the group has also said it would “never publish the data”).
